newsitem.title: BRAZIL: COFFEE--Rio meetings help to fuel price rally.
newsitem.headline: COFFEE--Rio meetings help to fuel price rally.

text.p: Rio de Janeiro lived up to its reputation as the "cidade maravilhosa" (marvellous city) this week, with the coffee market left marvelling at a string of announcements that helped push prices to new highs.

The week started with an declaration by Ivorian Minister for Commodities Guy-Alain Gauze that Vietnam, currently outside of the Association of Coffee Producing Countries (ACPC), was to consider joining the producer group.

The prospect of Vietnam's participation was enough to set robusta prices rising and even comments the next day from Vietnamese officials in Hanoi that membership was being considered but not imminent did not dent market optimism.

Gauze was participating in an international coffee seminar Jan 20-22 at which delegates were continually reminded of the possibility of a smaller Brazilian crop in 1997/98, another factor which helped also upward momentum to the market.
Probably of most importance was a reiteration by Brazil that its own working range was between 18 million and 20 million bags, down from a 1996/97 crop of 25 million bags.

"Suddenly many people from outside of Brazil were receiving these forecasts from specialists face-to-face and not through informal telephone calls and reports and it really started to sink in," a trader said.
One telling sign was the sudden interest at the end of the meeting in a trip being organised into the coffee areas, said Francisco Ourique, one of the conference's organisers.
"We had circulated information about the trip for the past two months and had only a few bookings. On the last day, we had to turn people down," Ourique said.

The seminar was followed by an emergency meeting of ACPC which had been requested by African producers seeking a 2.5 million bag cut in member exports in first half 1997 amid concern over the differential between arabica and robusta.

But a rise in arabica and more recently robusta prices which had taken place since the proposal was first made public in December led to suggestions that there was now less of a need to reduce member exports.
A political decision was made, however, to support robusta producers and members announced they would slice 1.3 million bags off shipments between January and June this year.
Of that total, 300,000 bags would be arabica.
Robusta producers, including Indonesia, will decide on individual country contributions at a meeting to be held in Bali on Feb 6.
Arabica producers will consult by telephone but with only 300,000 bags to share out, few difficulties were expected in dividing out the cut, traders said.
Despite the achievements of the past week, Rio de Janeiro is unlikely to host another series of coffee meetings of this stature at least for another two years.

The government has already said it would like to host another international seminar next year but this time in Sao Paulo while the ACPC also took another decision -- that in future all council sessions should take place in London.
